name: Uber
tagline: Uber's surge pricing is the most visible application of behavioral economics in everyday life — and the most publicly controversial.
key_insight: Uber is a case study in dual-sided behavioral design: the company applies behavioral science to both riders (friction elimination, surge anchoring) and drivers (gamification, loss aversion goals). The ethical tension is asymmetric — riders benefit from reduced friction, but drivers are nudged to work longer hours in ways that may not serve their interests. Uber's behavioral design works precisely because it's invisible: users don't know they're being nudged, and drivers don't realize the earnings goal is an anchor, not a recommendation.
top_evidence: Removing surge multiplier and showing only total fare reduced acceptance (leaked NYT 2017). Drivers exhibit strong reference-dependent behavior (Chen et al. 2019).

techniques.title: Surge Pricing as Dynamic Anchoring
techniques.description: Uber's surge pricing uses reference dependence brilliantly. Users have a mental anchor for 'normal' price. When surge pricing shows '2.3x', users evaluate the price relative to their anchor — not relative to the absolute cost of the trip. After surge drops to '1.2x', it feels like a deal even if it's still more expensive than a traditional taxi. The surge multiplier creates a reference frame that makes non-surge prices feel like gains.
techniques.evidence: Kahneman & Tversky's Prospect Theory: people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point, not in absolute terms. Uber's own research (leaked to NYT, 2017): removing the surge multiplier and showing only the total fare reduced acceptance rates — users needed the reference frame to evaluate 'fairness.'

techniques.title: One-Tap Ride Request: Friction Elimination
techniques.description: Uber reduced the entire taxi-hailing process (find taxi → negotiate → pay cash → tip) to a single button press. This radical friction elimination is CLT in action: by minimizing extraneous cognitive load (no mental math, no cash handling, no tipping anxiety), users can hail rides impulsively. The easier it is to do something, the more people do it.
techniques.evidence: Before Uber, hailing a taxi in NYC involved 5+ decision points. Uber reduces this to 2 (enter destination, confirm pickup). Uber's 2016 Economic Impact Report: ride frequency increased 3x compared to pre-Uber taxi usage in comparable demographics.

techniques.title: Driver Gamification: Earnings Goals as Anchoring
techniques.description: Uber shows drivers a daily earnings goal and uses progress indicators (you're $23 away from $200 today!). This exploits loss aversion — stopping before reaching the goal feels like a loss. Combined with 'quest' bonuses (complete 3 more rides for $15 extra), Uber creates a behavioral architecture where drivers work longer than they might otherwise choose to.
techniques.evidence: Chen et al. (2019, Uber driver study): drivers exhibit strong reference-dependent behavior, working significantly longer on days when they haven't reached their earnings target. The labor supply curve bends the 'wrong' way from classical economics — because loss aversion overrides rational time-value calculation.

strengths: Friction elimination for riders is genuinely life-improving
weaknesses: Driver gamification optimizes for Uber's supply, not driver wellbeing
Earnings goals use loss aversion unrecognizably
